props.title: Murder on a Sunday Morning
props.initialSlug: Innocence on trial. Justice on the line.

sections.content: **Murder on a Sunday Morning (2001)** (2001) revolutionized true-crime documentary filmmaking by meticulously following public defender Patrick McGuinness as he fights to prove the innocence of 15-year-old Brenton Butler, wrongly accused of murder in Jacksonville, Florida. The Oscar-winning film exposes deep-rooted issues in the American justice system, particularly racial profiling and coerced confessions. Director Jean-Xavier de Lestrade's unflinching camera captures every devastating moment, from Butler's traumatic interrogation to McGuinness's masterful courtroom strategy, setting a new standard for legal documentaries that would influence works like **The Staircase** (2004) and **Making a Murderer** (2015).

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a turning point for social justice documentaries, with films like **Murder on a Sunday Morning** (2001) and **The Central Park Five** (2012) forcing audiences to confront systemic racism in law enforcement. These films share DNA with earlier works like **In the Name of the Father** (1993), but their direct-cinema approach and focus on contemporary cases created immediate real-world impact. De Lestrade's technique of embedding with the defense team established a template for modern true-crime storytelling. SUBHEAD: Impact on Legal Documentary Filmmaking

The film's influence extends beyond its immediate subject matter. Its success helped spawn a wave of criminal justice documentaries that prioritize process over sensationalism. **Strong Island** (2017) and **Time** (2020) follow this tradition, examining how race, class, and institutional power intersect in American courtrooms. De Lestrade's approach - allowing the legal proceedings to build tension naturally while revealing character through observed moments - became the gold standard for courthouse documentaries.
